analysis.one_liner: Requires industrial plants to monitor toxic air emissions at their property lines and publishes the data publicly.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by 17 House Democrats, was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the EPA to identify at least 100 industrial facilities with the highest hazardous air pollution risks — chemical, petroleum, paper, and metals plants among them — and install fenceline monitoring at their property boundaries. It would require companies to measure and electronically report toxic emissions like ethylene oxide, benzene, and formaldehyde, publish the data in multiple languages within days, and trigger corrective action when pollution at the fenceline exceeds health-protective levels. It would also expand the national air monitoring network with 80 new stations and at least 1,000 low-cost air sensors, prioritized for communities with high asthma, poverty, or nearby major polluters.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near industrial polluters — especially communities with high cancer risk, asthma rates, or poverty — would get real-time, publicly available data on the toxic chemicals crossing their neighborhoods' air, plus enforceable requirements on facilities to investigate and fix exceedances.

how_it_helps.text: Requires EPA to identify and monitor at least 100 high-priority sources of hazardous air pollutants, drawing from facilities the EPA Inspector General flagged for high cancer risk, and maintain fenceline monitoring for at least 6 years [S2] [S3].

Requires plants in affected source categories to run continuous monitoring with at least 95% data reliability, exceed a public 'corrective action level' at the fenceline triggering root-cause analysis, remediation, and a public violation report [S3].

Mandates EPA publish all monitoring data in multiple languages within 7 days of submission, publicize it through local media near each facility, and offer community alert signups when pollution exceeds health reference levels [S3].

Directs deployment of at least 1,000 air quality sensors in clusters of five or more, prioritized toward census tracts with elevated asthma, poverty, or nearby major pollution sources, and 80 new multipollutant monitoring stations plus 100 reference monitors in undermonitored areas [S2] [S3].
Authorizes roughly $277 million for fiscal years 2023-2024 to fund the monitoring programs and network expansion [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Chemical, petroleum, plastics, paper, and metals manufacturers facing fenceline monitoring mandates, corrective action when pollution crosses health thresholds, and public violation reporting — plus the federal Treasury for the authorized $277 million.

drawbacks.text: Monitoring equipment, corrective action, and emergency-response monitoring impose real compliance costs on industrial facilities, some of which would likely flow into consumer prices [S3].

The 1,000 required sensors are capped at $5,000 each, and low-cost sensors are generally less accurate than reference-grade monitors; the bill handles this by using sensor data only to trigger installation of reference monitors, but accuracy limits remain a legitimate concern [S3].
The bill authorizes about $277 million in new federal spending over two years for the monitoring networks [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of Americans living downwind of chemical and petroleum facilities, the bill's benefit is unusually concrete: measured, published, near-real-time data on the exact pollutants the EPA's own Inspector General has flagged for high cancer risk, with an enforceable trigger to force cleanup. The compliance costs fall on a concentrated set of facilities, and federal costs are modest against the scale of the network buildout. The main honest weakness is sensor accuracy at the low-cost end, which the bill mitigates but does not eliminate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and stayed there — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — until the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lisa Blunt Rochester introduced the bill on July 13, 2022, with 7 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce that same day [S1] [S3] [S5].
Sixteen additional Democratic members cosponsored the bill [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no committee markup, and no floor action after the initial referral through the end of the 117th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical, petroleum, and other industrial facilities avoid the monitoring mandates and corrective-action obligations the bill would have imposed, and the communities near those facilities never receive the fenceline data the bill would have produced. The House committee structure that allowed the bill to sit without action is also better off.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 16 cosponsors

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — through the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: All 17 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Democratic-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would require continuous fenceline and emergency monitoring, public reporting of toxic emissions, and corrective action when pollution exceeds health thresholds — the same facilities it targets profit today in part because their emissions are not directly measured at the property line. Its public health benefit runs against the industry's cost-avoidance interest.

industries.industry: Petroleum refiners and marine cargo operations
industries.note: Explicitly listed in the bill's covered source categories; would bear fenceline monitoring costs and public violation reporting [S3].

industries.industry: Paper, metals, and hazardous waste industries (NAICS 322, 331, 332, 339, 562)
industries.note: Covered source categories under the bill's monitoring and corrective-action requirements where they are major or area sources of hazardous air pollutants [S3].
The bill mandates purchase of continuous monitors, at least 1,000 sensors, and a major monitoring network buildout, creating a large guaranteed market for monitoring equipment [S3].
